title: Karpathy in an hour
pitch: The best parts of six Karpathy talks, from Software 2.0 to Software 3.0.
q: Build a 60-minute watch plan: the essential Andrej Karpathy, across his talks here (Intro to Large Language Models, Building the Software 2.0 Stack, Software Is Changing (Again), AI for Full-Self Driving at Tesla, the CVPR'21 keynote, No Priors Ep. 80). Use 5 to 7 segments from at least 4 different videos, at most 2 from any one video, each at least 3 minutes long, in an order where each builds on the last. For each segment give a short heading naming the video, its length in whole minutes, and one line on why it matters. Don't write timestamps or seconds yourself; the citation marks where each segment starts. End with the total time.
stream:
data: {"type":"response.output_text.delta","delta":"1. **Intro to Large Language Models — the model, training, and inference** — *about 10 min* 
 Establishes what an LLM is, how next-token prediction compresses knowledge, and why training is far more demanding than running the finished model. [1]

2. **Building the Software 2.0 Stack — optimization becomes programming** — *about 10 min* 
 Moves from hand-written programs to defining a search space, letting optimization discover the code, and seeing data-labeling as a core programming activity. [2]

3. **AI for Full-Self Driving at Tesla — neural networks in the real world** — *about 10 min* 
 Applies Software 2.0 to autonomy: vision-based driving, long-tail edge cases, fleet data, and the iterative data engine needed for production. [3]

4. **CVPR’21 Keynote — the data engine at scale** — *about 10 min* 
 Deepens the production lesson through large, clean, diverse datasets, auto-labeling, shadow mode, hard-example mining, and massive training infrastructure. [4]

5. **Software Is Changing (Again) — Software 3.0** — *about 10 min* 
 Generalizes the progression from code to weights to prompts, showing why LLMs make neural networks programmable in natural language. [5]

6. **No Priors Ep. 80 — from AI capability to useful products** — *about 10 min* 
 Concludes with the practical frontier: using AI as the student-facing layer of education while distinguishing impressive demos from reliable products. [6]

**Total: about 60 minutes.**"}

title: Talks every programmer should watch, in 45 minutes
pitch: Hickey, Feldman, Bret Victor, the event loop and Erlang: only the parts HN keeps quoting.
q: Build a 45-minute watch plan from the programming talks Hacker News tells every developer to watch: The Value of Values (Rich Hickey), Making Impossible States Impossible and Why Isn't Functional Programming the Norm (Richard Feldman), All the Little Things (Sandi Metz), The Future of Programming (Bret Victor), What the heck is the event loop anyway, The Soul of Erlang and Elixir. Pick the single strongest idea from each, not intros. Use 5 to 7 segments from at least 4 different videos, at most 2 from any one video, each at least 3 minutes long, in an order where each builds on the last. For each segment give a short heading naming the video, its length in whole minutes, and one line on why it matters. Don't write timestamps or seconds yourself; the citation marks where each segment starts. End with the total time.
stream:
data: {"type":"response.output_text.delta","delta":"### 1. **The Value of Values — 8 min**
Immutable values can be shared safely, make results reproducible, and create interfaces that reduce coordination between systems. [1]

### 2. **Making Impossible States Impossible — 6 min**
Design the data model so invalid states cannot be represented, turning debugging problems into compiler errors. [2]

### 3. **Why Isn’t Functional Programming the Norm? — 6 min**
Functional style is spreading even through mainstream languages—not because FP has won outright, but because avoiding mutation and side effects is increasingly seen as a baseline advantage. [3]

### 4. **The Future of Programming — 7 min**
The best abstractions express goals and constraints, letting the computer determine the procedure rather than forcing developers to specify every step. [4]

### 5. **What the Heck Is the Event Loop Anyway? — 7 min**
Asynchronous code only helps when it keeps slow work off the call stack; otherwise rendering and user interaction remain blocked. [5]

### 6. **The Soul of Erlang and Elixir — 7 min**
Processes isolate failures and latencies, allowing the rest of a system to keep progressing when one computation crashes or consumes too much CPU. [6]

### 7. **The Soul of Erlang and Elixir — 4 min**
Once processes are isolated, the runtime can inspect, trace, and terminate a troubled process in a live system without taking the whole application down. [7]

**Total: about 45 minutes.**"}

title: From sand to software in 40 minutes
pitch: How a chip is made, how a CPU says hello, and the computers that came before.
q: Build a 40-minute watch plan on how computers actually work, bottom up: from manufacturing a chip (Indistinguishable From Magic), to building a CPU and running code on it (Ben Eater's 6502 and 8-bit computer), to analog signals (Digital Show and Tell), to mechanical computers (fire control computers) and the British home-computer race (Micro Men). Use 5 to 7 segments from at least 4 different videos, at most 2 from any one video, each at least 3 minutes long, in an order where each builds on the last. For each segment give a short heading naming the video, its length in whole minutes, and one line on why it matters. Don't write timestamps or seconds yourself; the citation marks where each segment starts. End with the total time.
stream:
data: {"type":"response.output_text.delta","delta":"1. **Indistinguishable From Magic — From fab to wafer** — *about 7 min* 
 Start with ultra-clean fabrication, single-crystal silicon, wafer scaling, and lithography—the physical foundation of every computer. [1]

2. **Indistinguishable From Magic — What a modern device looks like** — *about 4 min* 
 Now zoom into the transistor itself: nanoscale layers, channels, contacts, and the astonishing density that turns a wafer into a processor. [2]

3. **“Hello, world” from scratch on a 6502 — The clock and bus** — *about 13 min* 
 See a real CPU’s clock, address bus, data bus, reset behavior, and instruction fetches emerge from a chip on a breadboard. [3]

4. **“Hello, world” from scratch on a 6502 — Reset to program execution** — *about 5 min* 
 Follow the reset vector into the program counter, then watch the 6502 fetch and decode its first instruction—making “running code” concrete. [4]

5. **Digital Show and Tell — What digital signals really are** — *about 3 min* 
 Connect the CPU’s discrete operations to the physical world: sampling, reconstruction, Nyquist, and why a digital signal is not literally a staircase. [5]

6. **Basic Mechanisms in Fire Control Computers — Mechanical computation** — *about 5 min* 
 Step back before electronics to see computation implemented with shafts, gears, cams, and differentials—mechanisms that continuously combine changing inputs. [6]

7. **Micro Men — From chips to computers in British homes** — *about 4 min* 
 Finish with the practical consequence: cheap processors becoming affordable home machines, and the competition that pushed computing into ordinary households. [7]

**Total: about 40 minutes.**"}

title: Game feel in 30 minutes
pitch: Why some games feel great: screenshake, juice, and speedrunners bending the rules.
q: Build a 30-minute watch plan on game feel and game craft: The art of screenshake (Jan Willem Nijman), Juice it or lose it (Jonasson and Purho), the SM64 0.5 A presses run, reverse emulating the NES, and This Is Phil Fish. Show the moments where you can see the technique on screen. Use 5 to 7 segments from at least 4 different videos, at most 2 from any one video, each at least 3 minutes long, in an order where each builds on the last. For each segment give a short heading naming the video, its length in whole minutes, and one line on why it matters. Don't write timestamps or seconds yourself; the citation marks where each segment starts. Never use the same moment twice. End with the total time.
stream:
data: {"type":"response.output_text.delta","delta":"## 30-minute watch plan

1. **The Art of Screenshake — about 4 min** 
 Start with the deliberately dull shooter, then watch Nijman layer in animation, sound, faster fire rate, more enemies, larger bullets, muzzle flashes, and inaccurate shots—the clearest introduction to how tiny feedback changes transform game feel. [1]

2. **Juice It or Lose It — about 4 min** 
 See “juice” become a repeatable craft: squash and stretch, impact scaling, rotation, wobble, hit flashes, block reactions, and bouncing lines visibly turn simple Breakout interactions into expressive ones. [2]

3. **SM64 0.5 A Presses — about 9 min** 
 A progression from diagrams to live execution: sinking speeds, parallel universes, slope-dependent movement, and the final route demonstrate how understanding a game’s underlying rules can produce entirely new forms of movement. [3]

4. **Reverse Emulating the NES — about 6 min** 
 Watch the NES’s apparent limitations become design space: the Raspberry Pi cartridge concept, tile-based graphics, scanline timing, and dynamically changing colors show how technical constraints can be manipulated into new visual behavior. [4]

5. **This Is Phil Fish — about 6 min** 
 The Fez development section shows the power of instantly legible design: the game’s 2D/3D mechanic communicates itself in seconds of gameplay or a GIF, turning a sophisticated idea into a highly shareable visual moment. [5]

**Total: about 30 minutes.**"}

title: How everyday machines work
pitch: Toasters, dishwashers, heat pumps and a 1937 differential, explained on screen.
q: Build a 40-minute watch plan on the machines around us, explained: Technology Connections on the antique toaster, dishwasher detergent and heat pumps, the 1937 film on how differential steering works, and the mechanical fire control computer. Pick the moments where the mechanism is shown working. Use 5 to 7 segments from at least 4 different videos, at most 2 from any one video, each at least 3 minutes long, in an order where each builds on the last. For each segment give a short heading naming the video, its length in whole minutes, and one line on why it matters. Don't write timestamps or seconds yourself; the citation marks where each segment starts. Never use the same moment twice. End with the total time.
stream:
data: {"type":"response.output_text.delta","delta":"1. **Technology Connections — The Antique Toaster that's Better than Yours — about 6 min** 
 Start with a familiar appliance whose heating element doubles as its motor: levers, Nichrome-wire expansion, the bread carriage, and the thermostat all work together. [1]

2. **Technology Connections — Dishwashers Explained — about 6 min** 
 See the same idea at larger scale: a pump turns electrical power into rotating spray arms, while the sump, filters, valves, motors, and heater coordinate the wash. [2]

3. **Technology Connections — Heat Pumps: the Future of Home Heating — about 5 min** 
 Follow a working refrigeration rig as the compressor, condenser, metering device, and evaporator move heat by changing refrigerant pressure and phase. [3]

4. **Around the Corner — How Differential Steering Works (1937) — about 5 min** 
 The model makes motion intuitive: a pivoting crossbar lets one wheel turn faster than the other, then evolves into meshed differential gears driven by a power shaft. [4]

5. **U.S. Navy — Basic Mechanisms in Fire Control Computers — about 5 min** 
 Now see mechanical motion become numerical information through shafts, rack-and-pinion translation, gear ratios, and cams that turn rotation into controlled movement. [5]

6. **Technology Connections — Dishwashers Explained — about 6 min** 
 Return to the dishwasher for the control sequence in action: pre-wash detergent, fresh-water filling, the main wash, heating, rinsing, and drying show how timing is part of the mechanism. [6]

7. **U.S. Navy — Basic Mechanisms in Fire Control Computers — about 7 min** 
 Finish with the payoff: a differential combines changing inputs continuously, first in a rack-and-pinion demonstration and then in the rotating bevel-gear assembly used in fire-control computers. [7]

**Total: about 40 minutes.**"}

title: See the math: 35 minutes of visual intuition
pitch: Vectors, Fourier, Bézier curves and colormaps, each idea shown, not told.
q: Build a 35-minute watch plan for visual intuition in math: 3Blue1Brown on vectors and the Fourier transform, Freya Holmér on Bézier curves, Gilbert Strang's first MIT linear algebra lecture, and the matplotlib default colormap talk. Pick the moments where the picture makes the idea click. Use 5 to 7 segments from at least 4 different videos, at most 2 from any one video, each at least 3 minutes long, in an order where each builds on the last. For each segment give a short heading naming the video, its length in whole minutes, and one line on why it matters. Don't write timestamps or seconds yourself; the citation marks where each segment starts. End with the total time.
stream:
data: {"type":"response.output_text.delta","delta":"## 35-minute watch plan: visual intuition in math

1. **3Blue1Brown — Vectors: addition and scaling** · **about 4 min** 
 Start with vectors as movements, then watch tip-to-tail addition and scalar multiplication turn geometric actions into coordinate arithmetic. [1]

2. **Gilbert Strang — MIT Linear Algebra Lecture 1: the row picture** · **about 3 min** 
 See equations become planes in 3D, with their intersection revealing the geometry behind solving a linear system. [2]

3. **Freya Holmér — The Beauty of Bézier Curves: from interpolation to curves** · **about 4 min** 
 Nested linear interpolations visibly generate quadratic and cubic Bézier curves, then become weighted sums of control points. [3]

4. **3Blue1Brown — Fourier Transform: the winding machine** · **about 6 min** 
 Watch a signal wrap around a circle until matching frequencies produce spikes, making frequency decomposition feel mechanical rather than symbolic. [4]

5. **3Blue1Brown — Fourier Transform: from rotation to the formula** · **about 7 min** 
 The rotating complex vector, wound-up graph, and center of mass assemble into the actual Fourier-transform formula. [5]

6. **Matplotlib colormap talk — why visualization changes understanding** · **about 3 min** 
 Compare raw numbers with color-mapped structure, then see how a misleading default can distort interpretation and even slow diagnosis. [6]

7. **Matplotlib colormap talk — color as a linear projection and perceptual space** · **about 8 min** 
 Connect the earlier linear-algebra intuition to color: high-dimensional spectra project into a lower-dimensional space, where perception determines whether visual patterns remain truthful. [7]

**Total: about 35 minutes.**"}
